story.title: ICE Arrests Reach Nearly 50,000 in July, Highest Monthly Total During Trump's Administration
story.summary: In July, ICE arrests surged to nearly 50,000, marking the highest monthly total during Trump's administration. Texas and Florida were significant contributors, accounting for nearly 20,000 of these arrests. This increase follows substantial funding from Congress, allowing ICE to hire 12,000 new deportation officers and agents.

explore_lenses.label: What changed in ICE's enforcement approach?
explore_lenses.title: More community arrests and local-police partnerships
explore_lenses.summary: The July increase reflects a shift away from an arrest mix dominated by jail transfers toward more arrests in the community, alongside wider use of state and local partners. The available data also indicate that 287(g) partnerships became a larger operational component than a year earlier.

claims.text: In July, 6,500 arrests—about 13% of the total—were attributed to state and local agencies partnering with ICE, compared with less than 5% of ICE's monthly arrests a year earlier.

ICE describes 287(g) as a voluntary program under which designated state and local officers may perform limited immigration-enforcement functions under ICE supervision, including in jails, during routine duties, or by serving administrative warrants.
Mark Krikorian of the Center for Immigration Studies said the administration changed tactics rather than stopping enforcement and argued the new approach was more effective.

explore_lenses.uncertainty_note: DHS largely stopped publishing broad immigration-enforcement data early in the second Trump administration; the reported figures were provided by ICE to the Deportation Data Project and analyzed by AP.

explore_lenses.label: Who is being swept into the July arrests?
explore_lenses.title: Many were arrested outside custody and lacked charges
explore_lenses.summary: The July figures do not support a characterization of the arrests as limited to people with criminal convictions. They show substantial community enforcement, including people with no listed convictions or pending criminal charges.

claims.text: More than half of people arrested by ICE in July had neither a criminal conviction nor a pending criminal charge; fewer than one-quarter had been convicted of a crime.
Half of July arrests were non-custodial, meaning ICE arrested people in the community rather than taking custody of people already held by police or in prisons.

AP reported that ICE had begun arresting some Haitians after their protections from deportation were withdrawn; it also reported accounts of people with valid work permits and pending asylum claims being arrested during traffic stops.
An ICE administrative arrest is a civil immigration enforcement action, not itself a criminal conviction.

explore_lenses.label: What happens after an ICE arrest?
explore_lenses.title: Arrest does not by itself decide removal
explore_lenses.summary: An ICE arrest can lead to detention, release, or removal proceedings, but the path depends on the individual's legal circumstances. In standard removal proceedings, an immigration judge determines removability and any eligibility for relief; some people may also seek review of custody or bond.

claims.text: Removal proceedings generally begin after DHS serves and files a Notice to Appear, and an immigration judge then determines removability based on evidence from DHS and the respondent.
In eligible cases, an immigration judge may reconsider DHS's initial custody decision in a separate bond hearing; either side may appeal the bond decision to the Board of Immigration Appeals.
A person found removable may seek available relief from removal, and either the person or DHS may appeal a final immigration-judge ruling to the Board of Immigration Appeals.

Some people are subject to expedited or reinstatement-related processes rather than ordinary removal proceedings, and fear claims can trigger review by an asylum officer and, in specified circumstances, an immigration judge.

story_report.summary: ICE made nearly 50,000 arrests in July, with Texas and Florida accounting for nearly 20,000. State and local agencies partnering with ICE were attributed 6,500 arrests, about 13% of the monthly total and a substantially larger share than a year earlier. ICE has also hired 12,000 new deportation officers and agents, expanding its enforcement staffing. The arrests may lead to different immigration processes, but the available data do not determine who will be detained, released, granted relief or removed.

sections.heading: State and Local ICE Partnerships
sections.body: ICE describes its 287(g) program as a voluntary arrangement that permits designated state and local officers to carry out limited immigration-enforcement functions under ICE supervision. Those functions can include work in jails, during routine duties or through service of administrative warrants. Mark Krikorian of the Center for Immigration Studies said the administration shifted tactics rather than reducing enforcement and argued that the approach had become more effective.

sections.heading: Arrestees and Community Enforcement
sections.body: More than half of people arrested by ICE in July had neither a criminal conviction nor a pending criminal charge, while fewer than one-quarter had been convicted of a crime. Half of the arrests were non-custodial, meaning ICE arrested people in communities rather than taking custody of people already held by police or prisons. AP also reported arrests of some Haitians after deportation protections were withdrawn, as well as accounts of people with valid work permits and pending asylum claims being arrested during traffic stops; an administrative ICE arrest is a civil action, not itself a criminal conviction.

sections.heading: Removal Proceedings After Arrests
sections.body: Ordinary removal proceedings generally begin when DHS serves and files a Notice to Appear, after which an immigration judge decides removability based on evidence from DHS and the respondent. Eligible people can seek review of DHS custody decisions in bond hearings, and either side may appeal bond or final rulings to the Board of Immigration Appeals. People found removable may seek available relief, while some cases instead follow expedited or reinstatement-related procedures that can include review of fear claims.

related_stories.title: Darline Graham won the GOP primary runoff in South Carolina
related_stories.summary: Darline Graham won the Republican primary runoff in South Carolina, defeating Ralph Norman. Backed by Donald Trump, Graham aims to secure a full six-year term to replace her late brother, Lindsey Graham, in the Senate. She will face the Democratic nominee in the upcoming November election.

related_stories.title: CIA Director Meets Russian Intelligence Officials in Moscow, No Meeting with Putin
related_stories.summary: CIA Director John Ratcliffe visited Moscow for talks with Russian intelligence officials, but did not meet with President Vladimir Putin, according to the Kremlin. The spokesman indicated that while it is too early to assess the impact of such meetings on U.S.-Russia relations, they are viewed as a positive development.

related_stories.summary: Manchester City has signed teenage Moroccan midfielder Ayyoub Bouaddi from Lille on a five-year contract valued at $117 million. The transfer marks a significant addition to the Premier League club's roster as they continue to strengthen their squad.

related_stories.title: US Military Strike in Caribbean Kills Four Alleged Drug Smugglers
related_stories.summary: The US military conducted a strike on a suspected drug-smuggling boat in the Caribbean, resulting in the deaths of four individuals. This operation is part of a broader campaign that has reportedly killed at least 227 people across 68 strikes in the eastern Pacific Ocean and Caribbean Sea over the past year.
